changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the CV Austere & Disaster Medicine guide's crush-syndrome section: entrapment physiology, the 2-hour tourniquet/isolation threshold, the hyperkalemia treatment ladder, goal-directed fluid resuscitation, and austere renal-replacement bridging.

summary: Crush syndrome is won or lost before the limb is ever freed. A trapped limb sequesters liters of volume and a lethal potassium load behind an intact barrier; releasing the crushing force without preparation can convert a stable entrapped patient into a cardiac arrest within minutes. Resuscitate before you decompress, isolate when you cannot resuscitate, and treat the potassium as already lethal.

body.text: Why entrapment is a systemic disease

items: Phase 1 — Ischemia: sustained compression collapses capillary flow. Myocytes go anaerobic, ATP depletes, the sarcolemmal membrane fails. Calcium and sodium accumulate intracellularly while potassium, myoglobin, creatine kinase, phosphate, and uric acid build up behind a still-intact barrier.

Phase 2 — Reperfusion: releasing the crush restores flow and sweeps the entire toxic load into systemic circulation at once. Leukocytes migrate into the damaged muscle, generating cytokines and free radicals that cause further myolysis on top of the original injury.
Can develop after as little as one hour of entrapment with a large muscle mass involved.

body.text: Think about the moment of extrication, not just the moment of injury — decompression without preparation can convert a stable entrapped patient into a cardiac arrest in minutes.

items: Third-spacing: up to several litres can sequester into a single severely crushed extremity — injured muscle takes up fluid like a sponge.
The patient can look reasonably stable while entrapped, then crash within minutes of release — that blood volume was never available to the central circulation.
Reperfusion unmasks the hypovolaemia while simultaneously releasing vasodilatory and toxic mediators — a sudden combined distributive-and-hypovolaemic collapse.
Hyperkalaemia-induced arrhythmia is the second most common cause of death immediately after extrication or reperfusion, after haemorrhage.

body.text: Tourniquet and chemical isolation — the 2-hour threshold

rows: Extricate and resuscitate per standard crush protocol — early fluid resuscitation before and during extrication is the single most important field intervention.

Consider a tourniquet placed proximal to the injury before extrication if fluid resuscitation and monitoring are not available — isolating the limb keeps the toxic load out of central circulation until resuscitation catches up. Reassess limb viability and risk/benefit continuously; this buys time, it does not substitute for definitive care.

body.text: Potassium release from ischaemic muscle can push serum levels into cardiac-arrest territory within minutes of reperfusion, often before any lab can be drawn. Treat the ECG, not the number you don't have yet.

rows: Peaked T waves → widened QRS → loss of P waves → sine wave → arrest. Any of these in a crush patient at or near extrication = treat as hyperkalaemia until proven otherwise.

Calcium chloride 1 g IV (preferred centrally) or calcium gluconate 2-3 g IV peripherally — first and fastest if ECG changes are present. Antagonises the cardiac membrane effect; does NOT lower serum potassium.

Regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose (D50 25 g) to prevent hypoglycaemia; nebulised or IV albuterol as an adjunct; sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV if acidotic. None of these remove potassium from the body — they buy time.

Loop diuretic if urine output and renal perfusion allow; potassium-binding resin as an adjunct; dialysis is the only definitive removal method once renal function is compromised — plan evacuation accordingly.

body.text: If you expect a dangerous potassium load at the moment of release — long entrapment, large muscle mass, no monitoring — consider pretreating with calcium BEFORE extrication rather than reacting to the rhythm after it has already changed.

Crush resuscitation targets a much higher urine output than standard trauma fluid resuscitation — the goal is flushing myoglobin through the kidneys fast enough to outrun tubular obstruction, not just restoring perfusion pressure.

items: Start before extrication: IV crystalloid as soon as access is obtained, ideally before the crushing force is released — the single highest-yield intervention in the whole algorithm.

Fluid choice: large-volume normal saline risks hyperchloraemic acidosis on top of the metabolic acidosis already present; many protocols favour a balanced or low-potassium crystalloid and avoid potassium-containing fluids entirely until the rhythm and labs clear.
Target: urine output ~200-300 mL/hr — well above the 0.5 mL/kg/hr trauma standard. The volume does mechanical work (flushing the tubules), not just supporting blood pressure.

Adjuncts: mannitol and urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate have been used to reduce myoglobin's nephrotoxic tubular precipitation, though supporting evidence is mixed — neither should delay volume administration.

Austere adjunct: when IV access or fluid supply is the limiting factor, enteral resuscitation with WHO oral rehydration solution has been described as a bridge (adapted from burn-shock literature) — it extends capability, it does not replace IV resuscitation where IV access exists.

body.text: Austere renal replacement — bridge, not cure

items: Definitive renal replacement requires evacuation to a dialysis-capable facility. Field/austere management exists to keep the patient alive long enough to get there.
Medical bridge: repeat the hyperkalaemia cascade (calcium → insulin/glucose + bicarbonate) on a scheduled basis if evacuation is delayed, rather than waiting for the rhythm to change again.

Improvised peritoneal dialysis has been deployed historically in mass-casualty/disaster settings when formal haemodialysis capacity was overwhelmed — requires a trained provider, sterile technique, and a peritoneal catheter; buys clearance time in hours to days, not the rapid correction haemodialysis gives.

Fluid restriction once anuric: if urine output hasn't responded to goal-directed resuscitation and the patient is now anuric, shift from aggressive volume loading to careful fluid restriction to avoid iatrogenic pulmonary oedema while awaiting transfer.

body.text: The decision point isn't whether the patient needs dialysis — in established crush-related AKI with refractory hyperkalaemia, they do. The decision point is how long you can keep them alive with medical management while evacuation is arranged.

Before crush syndrome can be managed, the casualty has to survive the primary survey. MARCH reorders ABC around the actual order of preventable traumatic death: Massive haemorrhage (direct pressure, packing, tourniquets — treated before airway; a patent airway is useless if the patient exsanguinates first) → Airway → Respiration (tension pneumothorax, open chest wounds) → Circulation (shock recognition, IV/IO, blood products, TXA per protocol) → Hypothermia/Head injury (active warming, TBI assessment — hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy is the lethal triad). The extended MARCH PAWS variant adds Pain, Antibiotics, Wounds, and Splinting for prolonged field care.

buildNote: Tier 1 — a time-critical field/ED algorithm with concrete thresholds (2-hour tourniquet decision, 200-300 mL/hr UOP target). Complements hemorrhagic-shock-mtp (general trauma/MTP) and hyperkalemia-management (the general ladder) with the entrapment-specific physiology and timing decisions neither covers.
